b21ea78343004fa2: Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing.
CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection.

The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation.
That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17.
On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE.

“Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42.

After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned.

In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail."
Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected.

Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators, are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions.

“The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).”
This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added.
Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27532, which targets Veeam backup infrastructure.

So if you haven’t already patched vulnerable PAN-OS software, do so now - and investigate whether attackers have already gained access to your network. Check Unit 42’s indicators of compromise to assist with threat-hunting activities.®

23356c532d0e1e80: An "avalanche of vulnerability reports" is forcing curl to move lower-severity cases into public view, reserving private handling for high and critical flaws.
From October 26, low and medium-severity reports should be filed in the open source data transfer tool's public GitHub repository, maintainer Daniel Stenberg said.

"Security researchers in doubt can still submit the issue on HackerOne and we can tell them what severity we deem it to be. Over the last few years, over 90 percent of all submissions could quickly be assessed to be less than HIGH."
Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty scheme this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.
Stenberg has previously acknowledged that not all AI-assisted reports are bad, but the workload now demands another response.

"This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in. We see no end to them and we do not anticipate this flood to decrease within the next several months.

"We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster. We must act to survive. This is our next step in a survival strategy. It might not be our last. We aim to not drown."
Public handling would let more people assess reports, develop fixes, write advisories, and check for related problems before releases ship, Stenberg said.

Handling vulnerability reports publicly won't reduce the work per report, he admits, though it could spread the load and make the resulting lessons and documentation easier to find. At least that's the theory.
Public disclosure also gives attackers more time to exploit flaws before fixes arrive. The maintainer agrees this is unfortunate yet unavoidable.
"We limit this practice to less than HIGH for this reason: at least these problems are not terrible."
Stenberg said researchers using AI are generating unusual option combinations unlikely to occur in real applications, then treating minor discrepancies as vulnerabilities.

"We can't continue down this spiraling path with our sanity intact. We don't have the bandwidth, manpower or even will to handle a never-ending vulnerability reporting stream at this pace. I believe few software projects can stand this kind of prolonged high volume deluge for extended periods. Something needs to give way." ®
0c57b3daa3d9f88f: SHAH ALAM: The Selangor branch of the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry (KPDN) busted a suspected operation involving the mixing of subsidised cooking oil with used cooking oil.

The mixture was believed to be intended for resale to used cooking oil processing companies or through the black market for higher profits.
Selangor KPDN director Muhamad Hanif Asa'ari said the activity was uncovered during a raid at an unnumbered premises under Ops Tiris 4.0 (Integrated).
The operation was believed to involve supplies from parties suspected of holding valid scheduled controlled goods licences, he said.
The team found piles of boxes containing packet cooking oil and plastic packets that had been cut open.
About 15,900kg of cooking oil and equipment used in the activity, including a lorry, were seized. The total value of the seizure was estimated at RM133,950, he said in a statement.
A Myanmar man in his 30s who worked at the premises was also detained to assist investigations.
Muhamad Hanif said the case would be investigated under the Supply Control Act 1961 to identify those involved and trace the distribution chain for the subsidised cooking oil.

Individuals convicted of an offence under the Act face a fine of up to RM1 million, a jail term of up to three years, or both. For a second or subsequent offence, the penalty rises to a fine of up to RM3 million, a jail term of up to five years, or both.
Companies face a fine of up to RM2 million, rising to RM5 million for a second or subsequent offence, he said.

6ce4be8a42c4e2c3: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia says responsibility for resolving the Rohingya crisis should not fall on the country alone, but requires Myanmar's commitment and concrete action to address the root causes of the crisis and achieve a lasting solution.

Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said Malaysia would continue to support the effort through diplomatic engagement and humanitarian cooperation, alongside sustained support from Asean and the international community.
He said the issue of Rohingya repatriation could only be resolved by addressing the root causes of the crisis in Myanmar.

Malaysia continued to pursue diplomatic efforts at bilateral, regional and international levels to create conditions for the Rohingya to return to Myanmar safely, voluntarily, with dignity and sustainably, he added.
"At the bilateral level, Malaysia continues to engage with Myanmar to encourage measures that support the return of the Rohingya to Myanmar.

"Emphasis is also placed on guarantees of rights, protection and equal opportunities so they can rebuild their lives in their place of origin without discrimination or exclusion," he said in a written reply in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He was responding to Datuk Shamshulkahar Mohd Deli (BN-Jempol), who asked about diplomatic guarantees and mechanisms with the Myanmar government to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation of Rohingya refugees, as well as follow-up measures through Asean to address the root causes of the crisis and prevent it from recurring and burdening host countries.
Mohamad said Asean continued to uphold the Five-Point Consensus (5PC) as its main framework for addressing the crisis in Myanmar.

Efforts focused on three components of the 5PC: ending violence, expanding non-discriminatory access to humanitarian assistance, and promoting inclusive dialogue with all relevant stakeholders in Myanmar.

He said Asean Special Envoy on Myanmar Tan Sri Othman Hashim continued to push for meaningful implementation of the 5PC, maintaining Asean's efforts since 2021 towards a practical and lasting resolution to the crisis.

As a next step, Asean was also identifying additional initiatives to complement existing efforts, with the aim of securing Myanmar's acceptance and cooperation in restoring peace and stability in the country, he added.

"On the humanitarian front, Malaysia also supports Asean's efforts through the Asean Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management (AHA Centre) to assist people affected by the conflict in Myanmar.
"The AHA Centre coordinates the delivery of humanitarian assistance without discrimination through cooperation with relevant parties in Myanmar and, where necessary, through cross-border efforts.
"Asean also works with the United Nations (UN) and other international partners to extend the reach of aid and ensure it reaches those in need," he said.

e683e8056bf173c6: AS of now, 6.12 billion people, or 74 per cent of the Earth's population, use the Internet for communication, entertainment, education and work.
Once concentrated on messaging, banking, news, navigation, blogging, gaming and social media, video and music streaming platforms have made huge strides and drawn billions of subscribers.
Two billion more use the Internet for virtual classrooms while about 3.5 billion of the global workforce uses it for corporate communications and the knowledge and gig economies.

The Internet is the top wealth generator of this era, and now the true workhorses powering it have emerged: 12,260 data centres spanning 180 countries, some in town-like warehouses, some buried underground or inside cavernous mountains, and some hidden undersea.

The United States operates the most with 5,430 facilities, or 45 per cent of the global infrastructure, followed by the United Kingdom (564), China (443), Germany (532), France (391) and India (298). Malaysia is modestly catching up: 26 operators across 64 facilities, including those already operational, under-construction and planned.
From 2021 to this year, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority reported data centre investments of up to RM386 billion.

But in the US, the US$10 trillion artificial intelligence (AI) boom is roiled with project delays, panicky investors and a massive public backlash that might influence next month's midterm elections. There are already spirited protests against data centres worldwide, Malaysia included, over their effects on the environment, resources and energy degradation.

Here, the public, watchdogs and civil society have urged the government to ban data centres near residential areas, fearing that server cooling will siphon water from residential taps and agriculture plots.
Communities worry the AI boom will drive up electricity bills and stress the national grid, especially due to centres built near houses and schools.
By 2035, data centres are forecast to swallow up one-third of Malaysia's total energy consumption.
This explosive potential growth prompted the drafting of the Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill to regulate industry proliferation and shield energy and water supplies.
The bill, spearheaded by the Economy Ministry, will prescribe that investments add economic value while tackling adverse environmental impacts.
Reacting to the backlash, the Johor government rejected 30 per cent of applications for data centres in 2024 for poor sustainability planning and extreme water consumption.

In February, Putrajaya suspended non-AI data centres to conserve resources. While data centres are welcomed, the race to become a regional hub cannot ignore the numerous adverse side effects. Data centres cannot exist at the expense of the environment and infrastructure.
fe50629463dc94be: Microsoft is pruning OneDrive's Copilot options from File Explorer's right-click menu, though the AI assistant isn't being shown the door entirely.

The Windows giant will remove shortcuts for summarizing documents, generating FAQs, comparing files and images, explaining images, extracting text, and asking questions. The rollout begins in mid-November and is expected to finish by early December. "Ask Copilot" will remain.

Microsoft's September 2025 announcement of the feature said: "We are bringing the power of AI directly into your daily file management experience. With just a few clicks, Copilot can help you summarize lengthy documents, generate an FAQ, compare files, or answer questions about your file."

Users can still right-click a OneDrive file and select "Ask Copilot" to start a conversation with the file attached, or use the Copilot icon in File Explorer Home. The individual actions will also remain available in the OneDrive activity center.

Adding a clutch of Copilot options with identical icons did little to make an already crowded menu easier to navigate. In its message on the subject, Microsoft said: "We're simplifying how people use Copilot with their OneDrive files in File Explorer."
An extra click, yes, but at least you won't need a taller screen to view even more context menu options.

Microsoft has stated that it intends to adopt a more thoughtful approach to how and where its AI assistant turns up in its product line. In March 2026, Windows boss Pavan Davuluri said: "We are reducing unnecessary Copilot entry points." File Explorer's crowded right-click menu seems as good a place to start as any.

The File Explorer context menu is also undergoing an overhaul as part of Microsoft's attempt to make it less "cluttered and sluggish," to the point where users could opt to have it work a bit like it used to in Windows 10. ®
2619dd66ca60992a: PARIS: French prime minister Sebastien Lecornu on Tuesday vowed a "massive" police presence at fresh protests called for the coming weekend, as he faced criticism over the handling of recent street violence.

The eurozone's second-largest economy was rocked on Saturday by some of its worst rioting in recent years, just six months before voters head to the polls to elect a successor to president Emmanuel Macron.
Facing angry lawmakers in parliament, Lecornu acknowledged that the security response had fallen short and promised a stronger approach ahead of a new wave of protests.
"The deployment for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu said.
He accused ultra-left radical groups of forging an "insurrectionary plan" that led to the riots, which erupted on the sidelines of nationwide protests over the cost of living.

Images of clashes, mobs looting stores and public buildings set ablaze last weekend prompted several countries, including the US, China and Germany, to issue travel advisories for their citizens in France.
French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in Paris and some other cities, and Lecornu said new curfews would be imposed on Tuesday where needed.
Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, after mobs set fire to government buildings and shops last weekend.
'War films'

During the night, a helicopter flew over the French capital's Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a searchlight across the square to monitor compliance with the curfew.
"The sound of a helicopter at one in the morning is a bit oppressive," said Sylvain Courant, a resident of the Les Halles neighbourhood, another hotspot of the street violence.
"It's that thing you see on TV, in all the good war films," Courant said.
Macron, currently on a Gulf tour where he secured additional diesel supplies in an effort to bring down prices, has acknowledged shortcomings in the handling of the protests.
France's government is wrestling with high public debt and anger over soaring prices, and facing a strong challenge from the far right.
The unrest on Saturday broke out after around half a million people turned out across France to denounce the cost of living, following four weeks of school protests.
On Monday, several cities, including Paris, the southwestern city of Bordeaux and Nice on the French Riviera, introduced partial curfews.
A targeted curfew for minors was to be introduced in several districts of the southern port city of Marseille from Tuesday evening and at least through Friday, a source close to the matter told AFP.
'Wake-up call'
Security forces arrested a man believed to be connected to the ultra-left over the burning down of a historic town hall in Limoges, whose destruction has become a symbol of the violence.

Authorities have come under criticism from parties across the political spectrum, with far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen describing the unrest as a "wake-up call" that exposed a "profound crisis" of authority.
Investors have sold off French debt in recent weeks amid rising doubts about the government's ability to rein in spending.
Under pressure to support thousands of damaged or looted shops, the government said interest-free loans would be made available from Friday to all affected businesses, along with other measures.
Justice minister Gerald Darmanin said nearly 150 people had been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts.
He argued that a strong judicial response was necessary to prevent ordinary people from taking matters into their own hands.
"The justice system is being extremely firm," he said. "People with no previous criminal record are being sent to prison."
Some demonstrators were seriously injured. One man lost a hand to a police grenade. In the eastern city of Mulhouse, a 17-year-old girl lost an eye.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez offered to resign on Sunday, saying police "had lost control" during the unrest. Macron rejected his resignation.
Troops in Milan

Italy was preparing to send 500 troops to Milan as the government considered a wider crackdown.
US president Donald Trump has seized on the unrest in France to amplify his anti-immigration and anti-Islam rhetoric, as his Republican party faces strong headwinds in the upcoming midterm elections.

Several analysts countered that immigration was not a driving force in France's unrest.

481036bb5c740fdb: MILAN: The production of Italian pasta is under threat as a protest by truck drivers in the south of the country over soaring fuel prices and the cost of living blocks deliveries to factories.

"This means that most of Italy's pasta production has ground to a halt, or is close to," he said.

La Molisana, another producer based in the Molise region, said it had experienced a significant drop in production and had been forced to draw on its stocks of raw materials such as wheat and semola flour.
Italy's pasta supply chain last year generated €13.5 billion in revenue, the European House-Ambrosetti (TEHA Group) said in a report in September.

Vincenzo Aleccia, president of the Trapani trucking consortium in the western Sicilian port city, told Reuters that he knew the disruption was enormous but added that "it's a peaceful protest and it's for the benefit of the people," saying rising prices affected everyone.

"People were trying to grab whatever was left. I had to go to a nearby town, and I also stocked up on flour and the food we consume most," said Zineb Boutimah, 45, who lives in Locri, a town in the southern province of Reggio Calabria.

7c5d6a77c9ff4d2f: LONDON: Prince Harry has said he hoped to reconcile with King Charles and the rest of his family with whom he fell out when he moved to the US six years ago.

Harry, 42, the king's younger son, caused a huge rupture in the British royal family when he and his wife Meghan quit royal duties and moved to California in 2020 from where they were highly critical of the institution.
He has barely spoken to his older brother, heir Prince William, for years, and his family has only recently met up again with his father.
In an interview with GQ magazine, Harry, who recently relocated back to Britain with Meghan and their two children, said he wanted to patch things up.
'The most important thing is to reconcile'
"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile," he told GQ.
He said he could understand the fascination with his family's situation as people could relate to it.
"There's sibling disagreements, there's broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent," he said.
Some people might be inspired by efforts to reconcile and this could help their own relationships.
"And some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out," he added.
Harry's spokesman said those latter comments were not meant as a swipe at William or any other family members.
Harry, the Duke of Sussex, went on to tell GQ that while "scars stick around forever", he wanted to encourage everybody to let go of the past.
"For me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives than to continue with issues with family," he said. "It's not worth it," he said.
Harry says children 'loving' UK school
In the lengthy interview, Harry also discussed themes he has previously talked about, such as the impact of losing his mother, Princess Diana when he was 12 and his mental health struggles.
However, he also talked about why he had returned to Britain, saying that being able to put his children in a British school "has meant a lot to me".

"I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they've been in school for two weeks. They're loving it and it's just giving them a whole different experience".

He also said he hoped that his fraught relationship with the British press, which partly led to him leaving in the first place and has led to a number of lawsuits against newspaper groups, would now be better.
"My hope is that it will change," he said. "There have been some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that.

"As with everything else that's going on in the world, there's aspects of the past that I'm sure all of us, me, my family, some of the British press, that we'd all like to leave behind us and work for the greater good," he said.
f2ab6981ac29ae96: PETALING JAYA: Kerajaan melarang penyedia perkhidmatan kecerdasan buatan (AI) menggunakan data kerajaan atau rakyat untuk melatih model AI mereka, kata Menteri Digital, Gobind Singh Deo.
Menurutnya, perkara itu merupakan klausa dalam semua kontrak perolehan AI kerajaan dan syarikat AI juga tidak dibenarkan menyimpan data rakyat Malaysia selepas proses pemprosesan selesai.

"Garis Panduan Pengadaptasian AI Sektor Awam (GPAISA) juga mewajibkan agensi meminimumkan data serta menyembunyikan atau menyahnamakan data sebelum diproses oleh sistem AI," katanya dalam jawapan bertulis di Parlimen.
Beliau berkata, kementeriannya sedang menggubal Rang Undang-undang Tadbir Urus AI bagi memastikan wujud akauntabiliti berkaitan sistem AI.
Beliau menjawab pertanyaan Ahmad Fadhli Shaari (PN-Pasir Mas) bagaimana kerajaan memastikan data awam yang diproses syarikat penyedia perkhidmatan awan dan AI kekal di bawah kawalan Malaysia.
Hanya data terbuka yang tidak sensitif disimpan di awan luar negara

Gobind menjelaskan kerajaan hanya menyimpan data terbuka yang tidak sensitif dalam perkhidmatan awan berpangkalan di luar negara, manakala data kerajaan diklasifikasikan 'rahsia' atau 'rahsia besar' hanya boleh disimpan di pusat data kerajaan, bukan dalam sebarang perkhidmatan awan dalam talian lain.
Jelasnya, maklumat diklasifikasikan 'sulit' atau 'terhad' hanya boleh disimpan dalam perkhidmatan awan persendirian atau hibrid berpangkalan di Malaysia.
"Bagi data peribadi rakyat yang dikendalikan sektor swasta, pemindahan ke luar negara dikawal di bawah Seksyen 129 Akta Perlindungan Data Peribadi 2010 (PDPA), sebagaimana dipinda pada 2024."

Antara lain, seksyen dipinda itu menetapkan persetujuan daripada subjek data diperoleh bagi pemindahan data peribadi merentas sempadan, manakala bidang kuasa negara penerima juga mesti mempunyai undang-undang setara dengan PDPA Malaysia.

Gobind berkata, kerajaan turut mewajibkan penyulitan (enkripsi) terhadap data miliknya bagi memastikan penyedia perkhidmatan asing tidak dapat membaca kandungan data itu secara sepihak, walaupun jika diminta pihak berkuasa negara lain.
29584844a18ef934: OVER the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins .
Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.

The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence (AI), tasking AI agents with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge.
Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers.

Beginning around Oct 2, Fagerland found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world.

At a time of rising anxiety over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor.
"It's a new world now," said Fagerland.
Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorised extraction of data.
Deere said it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that sensitive information was accessed".
SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained.
Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors".
Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages.
One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange.
The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on Sept 25, they set their AI army loose against American, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites.
Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters.
As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities.

Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly US$5,000 worth of tokens, or about US$50 per successful hack.
Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims.

In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after hours of trial and error, trick the server into executing malicious commands.
"It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," said Fagerland. "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions.

In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not the intention".
The ability of agentic AI systems to autonomously discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world.
Rogue agents have hacked their way out of computer labs, broken into government websites, and engaged in unsanctioned social engineering attempts.
South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by well-publicised hacks attributed to AI-using cybercriminals.
Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums.
Fagerland said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision but it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that.
The writer is from Reuters

d03d74b1ab187f96: KUALA LUMPUR: Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) transactions rose 22.5 per cent to RM14.7 billion in the first half of this year, according to figures disclosed in a written parliamentary reply.

63d3123a5caf3b98: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has proposed that the World Health Organisation's Western Pacific Regional Office (WPRO) urgently pilot a pooled procurement project for selected medicines to strengthen drug security across the region.

Health Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said the proposal was urgent as countries across the region faced critical challenges from supply chain disruptions, market uncertainty and heavy reliance on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), with geopolitical conflicts worsening the situation.

"Regional diplomacy and solidarity today must be translated beyond mere expressions of good intentions. To protect the survival of health systems in the Western Pacific, we demand a strategic, bold shift in action focused on tangible, measurable results," he said in a Facebook post today.
Dzulkefly presented the proposal at a ministerial roundtable held in conjunction with the 77th WHO WPRO Regional Committee Meeting.
He said the pooled procurement pilot should cover selected medicines with sufficient supplier competition and clearly established shared needs, and be implemented transparently.

To support the mechanism, Dzulkefly proposed developing an Asean Medicines Security Dashboard as an early warning system linking pricing information with supply distribution, stock availability and manufacturing capacity.
He stressed that price monitoring alone could not guarantee medicine security.
Instead, he said the region needed a strategic manufacturing alliance, supported by joint investment initiatives, to address production gaps.
"To realise this major framework, it requires clear leadership from a lead country under the 2026-2030 Plan, complete with funding accountability and clear key performance indicators," he said.

At the domestic level, Dzulkefly said Malaysia had institutionalised pooled procurement across government health facilities, maintained a 3-month buffer stock of medicines and spearheaded the Asean Drug Security and Self-Reliance (ADSSR) initiative.
He added that Malaysia would continue to leverage global health diplomacy platforms to ensure uninterrupted treatment for the public.
bae49355d6c4e904: PETALING JAYA: Ketua Penerangan Parti Wawasan Negara, Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal, mendakwa Bersatu 'tikam belakang' Perikatan Nasional (PN) berikutan keputusan Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM) membatalkan pendaftaran PN.

a764bc2dcc57efa5: COCONUT farmer Sombat Chuekrod travelled more than 200km to join hundreds on the streets of Bangkok last Friday demanding that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank change how they deal with the developing world.

Finance ministers, central bank governors and other top policymakers had gathered in the Thai capital for the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, to tackle an inflation crisis fuelled by the United States war on Iran and other economic shocks.
The message from the IMF has been clear: after years of economic crises, worldwide debt is too high and governments need to cut spending.
For the hundreds at the protest in Bangkok, as well as for rights groups and analysts, that message is the wrong one.
"We want the IMF and World Bank to rethink their role," said 51-year-old Sombat, as he walked alongside banners demanding reform of the institutions.
"Thai people are already poor. Please don't make them any poorer."
Protest organisers called on institutions like the IMF to focus on climate financing and tax reforms that aid poorer citizens rather than demand governments cut subsidies and social spending.

"Governments across the Global South are being forced to squeeze vital spending on public health, education, and social protection just to service illegitimate debts to wealthy nations and private creditors," said Lidy Nacpil, one of the protest organisers, in a statement.

Oxfam executive director Amitabh Behar said the world was facing an "inequality emergency", and that the IMF's calls for fiscal consolidation were code for cutting spending on essential social support during the war-fuelled inflation crisis.
"It will lead to (more) price rises. It might lead to hunger."

The IMF last week upgraded its world economic outlook, citing unexpected "resilience" in economic growth. But it warned that prosperity was fragmented, with vulnerable countries falling even further behind.
It highlighted oil-importing low-income countries not exposed to the boom in artificial intelligence investment as being the most vulnerable.
Yet the IMF's advice to all countries at a time of rising global debt levels has been to cut spending and rebuild fiscal buffers after years of spending on crises.

Asked what vulnerable countries should do, IMF deputy chief of research Petya Koeva Brooks said they had "no other choice" but to address their fiscal balances by either cutting spending or increasing revenues.

The IMF has proposed making energy and food subsidies offered in the wake of the Iran war more targeted, even as the United Nations Development Programme warned that if such subsidies were cut entirely, it could plunge 130 million people into poverty.
Protest organiser Nacpil questioned in an interview how one could draw a line between who deserves a subsidy and who does not.
"How poor do you have to be for them to think that you will need some support?" she asked.
Reza Baqir of Alvarez & Marsal's Sovereign Advisory Services said he has experience with the difficult trade-offs policymakers in low-income countries face in such crises.

"During my time as Pakistan's central bank governor, I saw firsthand how difficult it can be for countries to balance the needs of the countries' citizens with the needs of the IMF programme," he said.

"At the same time, it also reinforced the importance of addressing domestic governance challenges, so countries can build their own resources and fiscal buffers, reduce their reliance on the IMF and support their citizens in a targeted and prudent manner."

Christina Segal-Knowles of the Rockefeller Foundation said developing countries are "effectively being given two bad options" — either take on debt at currently sky-high interest rates, or make extraordinary spending cuts and potentially give up on development goals.
She proposed a "growth and investment reset" that ramps up funding to countries in need as part of a set of measures designed to provide sustained support at concessional rates.
On the streets of Bangkok on Friday, protesters prepared to spend the night under a flyover.
"We are raising our voices because we believe that the network of citizens present here are key stakeholders in the negotiations," said activist Supaporn Malailoy.
"This is not merely a matter of borrowing money; it is about shaping the very structure and direction of the nation's development."

But this is hardly a new proposal. It has been under discussion since 2018.
Malaysia needs neither another round of deliberations nor another announcement without a clear outcome. It needs transparency, a policy decision and the political will to act.

In May 2018, during Loke Siew Fook’s first term as transport minister, the transport ministry sought public feedback on the minimum licensing age, with Miros and relevant road safety authorities involved. The exercise ran until September, but its findings have never been made publicly available through official channels.

I obtained a summary of Miros’s findings after requesting it two years ago. The results were mixed. The online exercise involved 4,005 members of the public and 11 experts, while a separate survey covered 4,158 respondents.

Although Miros reported majority support among online participants for raising the age to 18, many motorcycle riders and secondary school students opposed the change. Some students even suggested lowering the age.
The findings do not establish a blanket public mandate for change. They establish something more fundamental: evidence was collected and the public deserves to know what became of it.

The presentation also reported that 80% of boys and 86% of girls surveyed rode to school without a motorcycle licence. Of 181 boys aged 16, only three held one. Meanwhile, 58% of students said their parents did not stop them from riding.

These figures concern the students surveyed, not all Malaysian schoolchildren. Nevertheless, they expose a problem that raising the licensing age alone cannot solve. Even a 13-year-old can ride an illegally obtained “kapcai”.
Wong himself has cautioned that raising the age will achieve little without effective enforcement against underage riders.
Licensing reform must, therefore, go hand in hand with enforcement, parental accountability and controls over access to motorcycles.
The paper trail

On Oct 8, 2019, police proposed a new B3 motorcycle licensing category at the National Road Safety Council’s 60th annual general meeting. The proposal envisaged restricting young riders to motorcycles of 70cc or below, or low-powered electric alternatives, to curb illegal street racing and improve road safety.

Recorded as Item 9.4 in the meeting minutes, the proposal was referred to the transport ministry. Years later, the public is still waiting to learn whether it was seriously considered and why it produced no clear policy outcome.

On Nov 25, 2021, Miros’s board backed a related but distinct proposal to study restricting young riders to motorcycles below 90cc. Recorded as Board Paper LPM 2-52 under Item 52.4(2), it was approved by the board, including its then chairman Suret Singh.
One proposal concerned a licensing category; the other concerned research into engine-capacity restrictions.
Nearly five years later, the study’s status remains unclear. Was it completed? What did it find? Were recommendations submitted to the transport ministry? If the study was not completed, why not?

In August 2024, the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia (Suhakam) children’s commissioner Farah Nini Dusuki sought an update on the B3 proposal and urged the transport ministry and road transport department (JPJ) to expedite legislation addressing motorcycle purchases by unlicensed riders. She also highlighted the unresolved status of the Miros study.
A study endorsed by the board should not become an administrative mystery.
Human cost
Suhakam has highlighted the risks faced by underage motorcyclists, including 87 children aged six to 10 who died while riding motorcycles rather than as pillion passengers.
Children do not acquire motorcycles by themselves. Adults may purchase them, provide access or knowingly permit illegal riding. Sellers and the wider regulatory framework also warrant scrutiny.

Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001 addresses neglect likely to cause physical injury to a child, while Section 39(5) of the Road Transport Act 1987 addresses causing or permitting a child below 16 to drive. Their application depends on the circumstances and relevant legal requirements.
Parental accountability matters, but it must not become a substitute for institutional accountability.

The government should disclose the status of legislation reportedly being developed to regulate motorcycle purchases by unlicensed individuals, explain outstanding obstacles and provide a timetable. The problem extends beyond teenagers riding kapcai – unlicensed adults can also access more powerful motorcycles.
I call on the transport ministry, JPJ and Miros to:
Publish the 2018 survey. Release its methodology, detailed findings and recommendations, while protecting respondents’ personal information where necessary.
Account for Board Paper LPM 2-52. Confirm whether the study was completed, publish its findings and explain what action followed.
Disclose the proposed legislation’s status. Set a timetable for regulating motorcycle purchases by unlicensed buyers and establish enforceable safeguards.

Set a timetable for licensing reform. Decide whether to raise the minimum age to 18 and seriously consider the B3 proposal, alongside proportionate power restrictions for young and inexperienced riders, effective enforcement and meaningful parental accountability.
Wong deserves credit for returning the issue to the agenda. In my years covering Miros, I have seen board recommendations stall before reaching the ministerial table.
It remains unclear whether Board Paper LPM 2-52, or any recommendation arising from it, ever reached the transport minister in a form requiring a decision. That, too, warrants an explanation.

Research cannot improve road safety if recommendations fail to travel from the boardroom to the ministerial table. Nor can policy succeed if it exists only in announcements, meeting minutes and presentation slides.
Malaysia is not short of studies, recommendations or press statements. It is short of visible follow-through.
Publish the evidence. Account for the decisions made and those left unmade. Set a timetable and act. The public has waited long enough, and too many children have already paid the price.
Shahrim Tamrin is a sustainable transport and road safety activist and former Malaysian Institute of Road Safety Research board member.

563d51871bb60e96: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth.

For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification. openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation.

OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification.

Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei. It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream.

The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM. It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler. As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant).

Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download. Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler.

openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle, akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024, while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page: the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year, this is a "non-upstream kernel port."

There are five types of installation ISO available: Offline Standard, Offline Everything (a hefty 24.9 GB), Network Install (a still significant 1.5 GB), and two variants of the desktop "DevStation" version – a basic one at 3.3 GB and an "everything" edition at 25 GB.

We gave the DevStation a very quick whirl in VirtualBox. It boots into its own installation program called Heolleo, which offers the choice of Simplified Chinese or English. Installation took a while, as it automatically fetches updates as it goes. We ended up with a GNOME desktop configured for Chinese, but we opened Settings, typed "language" into the Search box, and picked English. After a reboot, we could read most of the desktop. Program groups and some other elements are still in Chinese, but it's navigable with a bit of guesswork. It's GNOME 49, with the Dash to Panel and Arc Menu extensions preinstalled for a slightly more familiar layout. Opening a terminal, we were greeted with:
It also offers the Deepin Desktop Environment, UKUI (as seen in Ubuntu Kylin), MATE, Xfce, and the Kiran Desktop Environment, which is a new one to us.

In places, the English-language materials for openEuler mention Chinese CPU makers rather than western ones – which is understandable, in context. Examples include processors from Hygon, a Chinese licensee of AMD designs, as well as Phytium and Kunpeng, which explain the Arm support on offer.

In the western world, the Red Hat user community responded to the end of CentOS Linux by building new free distros that stay as close as they can to their progenitor: the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux projects, rebuilt from Red Hat source code.

Then, when the IBM subsidiary restricted access to that source to its customers in 2023, the Rocky and AlmaLinux projects started to diverge. Rocky aims for the closest possible RHEL compatibility, and its most visible innovation is that it's built its own new build service. It also found a clever workaround to get Red Hat's kernel source code. AlmaLinux still targets RHEL compatibility, but differentiates itself by retaining older device support and older CPU architectures after Red Hat drops them.

Chinese vendors have responded very differently. Those offering CentOS Linux-based OSes clubbed together, dropped their rival versions and their UNIX compatibility efforts, and instead are working on new tools and subsystems. Much like European interest in digital sovereignty, this is in part due to the Trump administration. Half a decade after it was cut off from its upstream sources, the openEuler platform is thriving and growing, even if few in the western world pay any attention at all. ®
2821d70d5a348f2a: JAKARTA: Indonesians protested in several cities on Tuesday, raging against wildfires and a toxic haze that has made thousands unwell for weeks on end in a crisis that has engulfed Southeast Asia.
Demonstrations were called by students to display dissatisfaction with the government of president Prabowo Subianto, which marked its second year on Tuesday.

They railed against perceived ineptitude and corruption during protests in the capital Jakarta, but also in Bandung and Yogyakarta elsewhere on Java island, as well as Pekanbaru in Sumatra and Makassar in South Sulawesi.
Many pointed particularly to an inability to put out the fires that have ravaged vast swaths of Borneo and Sumatra islands since July.
"If we burn, you burn with us!" read a protest banner held up by a demonstrator in Jakarta.
"I have the right to breathe. Extinguish the fires immediately," said another.
Residents in the city of Palangkaraya, on Borneo, told AFP of their despair.
"This haze is really bad. Sales are quiet. Prices keep going up, but there's no income," said Melsi, a 40-year-old streetside drinks vendor.
She cried as she spoke to AFP.
"What can we do? We're the little people, we can't do anything but hope that the government will handle it," Melsi said.
'Beaten up'
Homemaker Sifra, 29, said her husband and two children have been coughing for a month.
"Even inside the house, the smoke gets in. Honestly, since the haze, my body aches, as if I've been beaten up. The immune system is down. I get coughs and colds easily," she said.

Sifra, who like many Indonesians has one name, urged the government to step up its efforts - echoing the call made by dozens who protested in Palangkaraya on Monday to demand the declaration of a state of emergency.

Police detained six activists who had draped Greenpeace protest banners from a monument on Jakarta's central Bundaran HI roundabout on Tuesday morning, before the student marches, according to Jeanny Sirait, a campaigner for the NGO.
One read: "Haze & Prabowo's Regime = National Disaster."
National Disaster Mitigation Agency spokesman Berton Panjaitan told journalists in the capital that more than 60,000 firefighters, including volunteers, were deployed in dousing efforts countrywide.
Forty-nine aircraft were available for water bombing and cloud seeding to make rain, although many have been grounded intermittently due to the haze.
The Nusantara Atlas wildfire monitor said on Monday the Indonesian blazes have burned more than 1.9 million hectares of land in the first nine months of 2026.
The fires have sent air pollution levels soaring as far afield as Kuala Lumpur and Singapore.
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, partly due to a particularly severe episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon.
a2992e89e4dd0443: PETALING JAYA: Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar dan empat individu yang mendakwa diri mereka sebagai undang Negeri Sembilan mempertikaikan pembatalan pelantikan 10 ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri (exco) pada bulan lepas.

Tunku Nadzaruddin menegaskan semula dakwaan beliau terhadap takhta, malam tadi, dengan mendakwa Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir bukan lagi Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan apabila pelantikan ahli-ahli exco berkenaan dibatalkan pada 20 Sept, maka tidak sah dan tidak berperlembagaan.

"Kami dengan ini mengurniakan limpah perkenan kepada Ismail Lasim selaku menteri besar dan barisan exco... untuk terus mengemudi pentadbiran kerajaan Negeri Sembilan," menurut kenyataan bersama dengan empat 'undang' berkenaan dan Tunku Besar Tampin.

Mereka mendakwa Tuanku Muhriz bukan lagi Yang Dipertuan Besar apabila suatu proklamasi sebelum ini, oleh individu yang mendakwa diri mereka sebagai undang, diterima dan diputuskan untuk 'dilaksanakan' oleh exco.
Negeri Sembilan tidak mempunyai barisan exco sejak 20 Sept lalu selepas 10 anggotanya dilucutkan jawatan kerana melanggar sumpah jawatan.

Setiausaha Raja Norazli Raja Nordin berkata perkara berkaitan adat Melayu, termasuk pemilihan, pelantikan, peletakan dan pemecatan Yang Dipertuan Besar serta Undang, terletak dalam bidang kuasanya menurut Perkara XVI Undang-undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan (UUTKNS).

Mengenai proklamasi pula, Jabatan Peguam Negara menarik perhatian kepada pandangan awalnya bahawa proklamasi 19 April itu adalah tidak sah kerana tidak mematuhi kehendak-kehendak mandatori Perkara 10 UUTKNS.
c6c2448352b870f1: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?”

Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes.

That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow.
Three ways to run AI

Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models:

A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change.
On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action.

An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn’t free inference; it’s control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management.

The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system.
Ownership is an operating discipline

Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn’t make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way.

One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive.

The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn’t a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it’s a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness.

Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment.
From deployment to value

HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload’s requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices.

In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization.
Measure what matters

Token consumption remains useful, but it isn’t a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity.

Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck.

For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn’t whether enterprises will pay for AI — it’s whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it.

a1bd1920d6256523: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia hopes Japan will continue providing defence assistance under its Official Security Assistance (OSA) programme in 2027 and beyond, with an expanded scope to strengthen the country's defence capabilities.
Defence Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the matter was discussed during his meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi on the third day of his working visit to Japan.

He said Malaysia expressed its appreciation to the Japanese government for assistance provided under the programme, including the supply of counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (counter-UAV) systems to Malaysia.

"Both sides also exchanged views on security developments in the Indo-Pacific, particularly the situation in the South China Sea, with Malaysia emphasising the importance of Asean unity in addressing regional security challenges and preserving peace and stability in the region," he said in a Facebook post.

The meeting also covered efforts to expand maritime cooperation, explore government-to-government (G2G) defence procurement arrangements and a proposal to hold annual meetings between the defence ministers of both countries, following his meeting with his Japanese counterpart yesterday.

Khaled said the discussions also touched on the longstanding educational ties between the two countries, including the establishment of the Malaysia-Japan International Institute of Technology (MJIIT) and the University of Tsukuba campus in Malaysia, in line with the spirit of the Look East Policy.

He added that Malaysia regarded Japan as a trusted strategic partner, with bilateral ties expected to strengthen further ahead of the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries in 2027.
4584e69ce7546bd6: PETALING JAYA: Bersatu has been accused of engineering Perikatan Nasional’s (PN) deregistration after losing its leadership positions, allegedly to pave the way for an alliance with Pakatan Harapan (PH).
Wawasan leader Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal accused Bersatu of betraying its coalition partner PAS by lodging the complaint that led to PN’s deregistration today.
“People know the real cause was Bersatu’s complaint after its leaders were democratically removed from their positions in PN,” the Machang MP said in a statement.
He accused Bersatu’s leaders of shedding crocodile tears over the decision, alleging they pursued a “scorched-earth” strategy to bring down the coalition rather than surrender control to PAS.
Wan Fayhsal pointed to negotiations between Bersatu and the PH-led Selangor government over a confidence and supply agreement as evidence of an emerging political realignment.

Earlier today, Selangor menteri besar Amirudin Shari said he would review the state government’s planned cooperation with Bersatu following PN’s deregistration, but insisted the arrangement would be with Bersatu and not PN.
Wan Fayhsal claimed similar cooperation was being explored in Melaka.

He also questioned the timing of the Registrar of Societies’ (RoS) decision to cancel PN’s registration, which came two days before a court hearing on an application to stay the coalition’s suspension.
"Why such a rush that they could not even wait another two days?" he asked.
Wan Fayhsal accused RoS of double standards, claiming it ignored complaints over Bersatu’s internal disputes but acted swiftly when the party complained about PN.
He also accused the Madani government of using administrative powers to weaken political opponents ahead of the Melaka state election and GE16.
He, however, did not address Bersatu’s claim that it was excluded from PN’s Supreme Council meeting on July 16.
Bersatu secretary-general Azmin Ali had earlier accused the PAS-led PN leadership of breaching the coalition's constitution by denying Bersatu the right to attend, speak and vote at the meeting.
Azmin maintained that Bersatu’s complaint to RoS was intended to ensure PN complied with its constitution.

cd31a4d7c5db02f0: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches.

Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment.

With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia.
Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al.

The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations.

But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos.

Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs.

Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure.

Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention.

Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. When AI agents cannot autonomously communicate across environments, their utility droops from autonomous problem-solvers to plain localised macros.

Containers are gaining because of the widespread embrace of AI-enabled applications. Eighty-five percent of IT executives polled by Nutanix’s most recent Enterprise Cloud Index survey think that AI is accelerating their organization’s adoption of containers in a meaningful way; 29 percent think it is speeding-up adoption “to a great extent”.

“AI is accelerating the shift to containers because machine learning models require strict dependency packing, while critical applications and data remain spread across both virtualised and containerised environments,” says Harsha Kotikela, Senior Director of Product & Solutions Marketing at Nutanix.

Agents are multi-tier by nature he explains. “Inference is typically GPU-intensive and container-based, while agents are often CPU-intensive and container-based, and existing enterprise applications and data largely remain in VM environments. The challenge is to bring these tiers together so agents can work with enterprise applications and data, without forcing migration or creating additional infrastructure silos.”

The application landscape, meanwhile, has become just as diverse. Many organisations simultaneously operate traditional enterprise applications running on VMs, containerised apps, distributed AI applications and intelligent agents, with workloads deployed across private cloud, public cloud, and edge. Each environment has its own management tools, operational processes, security rules and governance models.

“Management capability has struggled to scale up commensurately,” says Kotikela, but adding more consoles or building separate operational teams for every technology stack does not necessarily solve this complexity: “In many cases, it increases it.”

However, Kotikela challenges the notion that the predicament enterprises face in straddling the VM-container divide is intractable. Rather, the challenge is to move towards a unified operating model that allows them to operationalize agentic AI while retaining flexibility across their existing and new environments.

“Rather than trying to work around heterogeneity, the objective now should be to make heterogeneous environments operate consistently with purposeful policies,” Kotikela says. “This is where Nutanix's dual-native architecture comes in, enabling enterprises to operationalize agentic AI across container-based inference and agent workloads alongside existing VM-based applications and data, through a consistent operating model.”

The reality is that the VM-to-container migration trend is sluggish, Kotikela suggests. Few enterprises are starting from scratch with containers. Many have long-established business applications on legacy architectures, on top of which they are building container-based applications, but mostly not to replace what they already have running on VMs. Rather, they are prolonging their VM investment.

It’s customer interest that’s informed how Nutanix provisions a governed, dual-native architecture through its Nutanix Cloud Platform – NCP – which runs traditional VMs and containerised/Kubernetes-based AI workloads concurrently on a single, consistent infrastructure.

NCP’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure foundation unifies compute, storage, virtualisation and management across on-premises resources, public clouds and edge. It works in concert with Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI), which provides the software capabilities to deploy, govern, and scale AI workloads.

Technology partnerships are vital to building AI support functionality into Nutanix's AI portfolio, explains Kotikela. “Nutanix and NVIDIA work together to provide an integrated platform for enterprise AI, combining Nutanix’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure and software with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI software. Nutanix Enterprise AI simplifies the deployment, management, and secure operation of AI models, integrating with NVIDIA NIM and NeMo microservices to support enterprise AI inference and agentic AI workflows.”

Meanwhile, “Nutanix Kubernetes Platform provides the foundation for managing Kubernetes environments, while Nutanix Unified Storage delivers the high-performance data access required by AI workloads. Together, these capabilities help enterprises deploy and scale AI while maintaining control over their infrastructure, models, and data.”
Stacks of opportunity

“In an ideal IT world you do not want to have to manage two different operational stacks – but the world of IT is rarely ‘ideal’,” Kotikela points out. “So you have to approach the challenge from a realistic perspective. You cannot bend your current stacks to a different reality without the risk of something breaking, and there’s no sense in that.”

He adds: “A platform that unifies VMs and containers improves developer time-to-value by getting rid of those infrastructure silos, and providing a single control plane.” Rather than development teams having to manage separate pipelines for existing VMs and containerised applications, a unified platform “treats both as services of equal status and importance”.

NAI delivers a unified and secure platform to deploy, manage and scale AI workloads, Kotikela says. It gives enterprises governance over their agents and models, full visibility over token usage, and streamlines AI development with a straightforward interface that integrates with existing infrastructure.”
Giving agents agency

According to Kotikela the next phase of agentic AI will be measured by the ability to operate agents with governance, visibility and control: “That’s what we set out to solve with the newest NAI release. Release 2.8 continues to evolve NAI with new control and governance capabilities across Nutanix Agent Gateway and Nutanix Private Inference. This means organisations can run AI across VMs and containers, bridge public-cloud LLMs with private self-hosted models, and deploy AI where data already is.”

Kotikela adds: “When I speak to customers, they tell me they want the freedom to choose between frontier and open-source models based on performance and cost, as well as the flexibility to run AI workloads in the cloud for experimentation and move them on-premises when they need greater control over their data or have sovereignty requirements.”
Stitch in time

For Kotikela the biggest challenge going forward is “operationalizing agentic AI - bringing together all the components required to make it work - from GPUs and underlying infrastructure to Kubernetes, AI models, inference engines, and gateways. These components must work together seamlessly across cloud, on-premises, and edge environments. Integrating and operating this multi-tier architecture requires significant time and effort from developers, IT architects, and infrastructure teams, diverting resources from delivering business outcomes.”

This is where Nutanix delivers value, says Kotikela. “We’ve done the heavy lifting of bringing together the infrastructure and software components required to run Agentic AI - within a unified operating model across hybrid environments. This allows IT teams to focus less on integrating and managing the underlying stack and more on operationalizing AI to deliver business value.”

d803cd30290c796e: LONDON: Prince Harry has said he hoped to reconcile with King Charles and the rest of his family with whom he fell out when he moved to the United States six years ago.

Harry, 42, the king's younger son, caused a huge rupture in the British royal family when he and his wife Meghan quit royal duties and moved to California in 2020 from where they were highly critical of the institution.
He has barely spoken to his older brother, heir Prince William, for years, and his family has only recently met up again with his father.
In an interview with GQ magazine, Harry, who recently relocated back to Britain with Meghan and their two children, said he wanted to patch things up.
"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile," he told GQ.
He said he could understand the fascination with his family's situation as people could relate to it.
"There's sibling disagreements, there's broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent," he said.
Some people might be inspired by efforts to reconcile and this could help their own relationships.
"And some people don't want it to work out. I want it to work out," he added.
Harry's spokesperson said those latter comments were not meant as a swipe at William or any other family members.
Harry, the Duke of Sussex, went on to tell GQ that while "scars stick around forever", he wanted to encourage everybody to let go of the past.
"For me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives than to continue with issues with family," he said. "It's not worth it."
In the lengthy interview, Harry also discussed themes he has previously talked about, such as the impact of losing his mother Princess Diana when he was 12 and his mental health struggles.
But he also talked about why he had returned to Britain, saying that being able to put his children in a British school "has meant a lot to me."

"I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they've been in school for two weeks. They're loving it and it's just giving them a whole different experience."

He also said he hoped that his fraught relationship with the British press, which partly led to him leaving in the first place and has led to a number of lawsuits against newspaper groups, would now be better.
"My hope is that it will change," he said. "There have been some battles that have been fought, necessarily so. But hopefully we can all draw a line under that.

"As with everything else that's going on in the world, there's aspects of the past that I'm sure all of us, me, my family, some of the British press, that we'd all like to leave behind us and work for the greater good."

49e3e073642015fe: PETALING JAYA: Teachers must be trained to respond promptly and intervene effectively to every bullying complaint so as to prevent lasting harm to victims, says education minister Fadhlina Sidek.
Speaking at an anti-bullying programme in Kuala Lumpur, Fadhlina said teacher training must be strengthened to ensure every case is handled comprehensively and appropriate action taken.

“Teachers must be trained in how to respond, including how to read situations, assess the circumstances of victims and bullies, and carry out ecological interventions to ensure all parties move in step,” Bernama quoted her as saying.
A total of 4,289 bullying cases were recorded across schools and boarding schools from March to August – or an average of 24 cases per day.
Fadhlina said bullying must be addressed through an integrated approach involving teachers, school administrators, district education offices, state education departments and the education ministry.
She said trainee teachers must also be taught character development so that they can shape students’ personalities and help tackle bullying in schools.
Fadhlina said the decline in parental support for children’s education, as highlighted in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results, also required serious attention.

She said a lack of support at home could affect the education ecosystem and students’ wellbeing, adding that parents needed to take a more active role in understanding their children’s experiences at school.

Meanwhile, law and institutional reform minister Azalina Othman Said stated that the Anti-Bullying Tribunal had received 68 complaints between June 17 and Oct 19, of which 51 had been resolved and 17 remained pending.
Speaking at the same programme, Azalina said 42 of the complaints involved victims aged 13 to 17, while 22 concerned children aged seven to 12. The remaining involved children aged four to six.
Students must first seek resolution through their schools, after which cases can be brought to the tribunal for mediation, formal apologies, counselling, or compensation orders.

Earlier this month, the education ministry said of the 4,289 bullying cases recorded from March to August, 2,480 involved physical bullying, 1,386 verbal bullying, 243 non-verbal bullying and 180 cyberbullying.
