1e30a53d9cdba92b: The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.”

A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster.

Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? That’s a question Polestar is trying to answer with researchers at the University of Oxford.
453597ae6c05a579: JAKARTA: Indonesians protested in several cities on Tuesday, raging against wildfires and a toxic haze that has made thousands unwell for weeks on end in a crisis that has engulfed Southeast Asia.
Demonstrations were called by students to display dissatisfaction with the government of President Prabowo Subianto, which marked its second year on Tuesday.

They railed against perceived ineptitude and corruption during protests in the capital Jakarta, but also in Bandung and Yogyakarta elsewhere on Java island, as well as Pekanbaru in Sumatra and Makassar in South Sulawesi.
Many pointed particularly to an inability to put out the fires that have ravaged vast swaths of Borneo and Sumatra islands since July.
"If we burn, you burn with us!" read a protest banner held up by a demonstrator in Jakarta.
"I have the right to breathe. Extinguish the fires immediately," said another.
Residents in the city of Palangkaraya, on Borneo, told AFP of their despair.
"This haze is really bad. Sales are quiet. Prices keep going up, but there's no income," said Melsi, a 40-year-old streetside drinks vendor.
She cried as she spoke to AFP.
"What can we do? We're the little people, we can't do anything but hope that the government will handle it," Melsi said.
Homemaker Sifra, 29, said her husband and two children have been coughing for a month.
"Even inside the house, the smoke gets in. Honestly, since the haze, my body aches, as if I've been beaten up. The immune system is down. I get coughs and colds easily."

Sifra, who like many Indonesians has one name, urged the government to step up its efforts – echoing the call made by dozens who protested in Palangkaraya on Monday to demand the declaration of a state of emergency.

Police detained six activists who had draped Greenpeace protest banners from a monument on Jakarta's central Bundaran HI roundabout on Tuesday morning, before the student marches, according to Jeanny Sirait, a campaigner for the NGO.
One read: "Haze & Prabowo's Regime = National Disaster."
National Disaster Mitigation Agency spokesman Berton Panjaitan told journalists in the capital more than 60,000 firefighters, including volunteers, were deployed in dousing efforts countrywide.
Forty-nine aircraft were available for water bombing and cloud seeding to make rain, although many have been grounded intermittently due to the haze.
The Nusantara Atlas wildfire monitor said on Monday the Indonesian blazes have burned more than 1.9 million hectares of land in the first nine months of 2026.
The fires have sent air pollution levels soaring as far afield as Kuala Lumpur and Singapore.
Indonesia experiences fires every dry season, but this year's blazes have been particularly severe, partly due to a particularly severe episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon.

fed74bf54807e3db: PETALING JAYA: The government bars artificial intelligence (AI) service providers from using data from the government or the people to train their AI models, says digital minister Gobind Singh Deo.

In a written parliamentary reply, Gobind said this is a clause in all of the government's AI procurement contracts, adding that AI firms are also not allowed to store data from Malaysians after processing.
"The guidelines on AI use in the public sector also makes it mandatory for all government agencies to minimise, conceal or anonymise data before processing them with AI systems," he said.
He added that the ministry is drafting an AI governance bill to ensure accountability when it comes to AI systems.
The minister was responding to Ahmad Fadhli Shaari (PN-Pasir Mas) who asked how the government was ensuring public data processed by cloud and AI firms remain under Malaysia's control.
Only non-sensitive, open data stored in foreign clouds

Gobind said the government only stores non-sensitive, open data in foreign-based data clouds, while secret and top secret government data can only be stored in government data centres, not just any online cloud.
On the other hand, confidential and restricted information can only be stored in personal or hybrid clouds based in Malaysia, he said.
"For personal data handled by the private sector, relocating it to foreign clouds is regulated by Section 129 of the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), as amended in 2024," he said.

Among others, the amended section requires consent to be granted by subjects for the cross-border transfer of their personal data, while receiving jurisdictions must have a law similar to Malaysia's PDPA in place.

Gobind said the government also mandates encryption of its data to ensure foreign service providers are incapable of unilaterally accessing the data, even if requested by the authorities of other nations.

00ca37e120856345: FRANCE is counting the cost of some of its worst unrest in years at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services.
HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT STOP MORE VIOLENCE AND HELP VICTIMS?
Authorities say 2,500 people are in custody awaiting questioning while 149 are detained awaiting trial.
Partial curfews have been imposed in parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Lille, Lyon, Nice and Marseille to keep the streets quiet in areas worst-hit by rioting.
The government, which had 60,000 officers mobilised at the weekend, plans to increase police numbers on the ground.
For businesses and victims of violence, the government is implementing state-financed furlough measures to avoid layoffs, and providing funds to help companies meet cashflow needs.
Insurers have promised speedy payouts to cover some of the damage, which hit more than 3,000 shops.
HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT ADDRESS UNDERLYING COMPLAINTS?
France's extremely strained public finances mean the government has precious little room for broader measures to address protesters' anger over the rising cost of living.
It has already hiked emergency spending this year to help certain sectors like farmers, fishermen and haulers cope with high fuel costs caused by the Iran war.
The ​protests began last month at high schools in Paris' ​working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and ⁠shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement.
The government has so far not committed to substantial extra funding for schools but has pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are qualified but not yet working, to fill staffing gaps.
HAVE PROTESTS PEAKED?

Cities were quieter at the start of the week. But some protesters have called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday. Unions have called for strikes on November 5 to protest budget cuts and support hiking wages.
Schools are on a break for two weeks, but some student organisations are calling for more demonstrations.
HOW WILL FRANCE'S DIRE ECONOMIC SITUATION BE AFFECTED?
The unrest is a blow to business confidence, which was already fragile due to a fiscal crisis and high energy prices.

The minority government is struggling to pass spending cuts in a divided parliament as part of its 2027 budget and is at risk of being toppled by opposition parties if a compromise cannot be found with at least some of them.
The government wants to cut its budget deficit to five per cent of economic output next year from 5.4 per cent this year – one of the biggest in the euro zone.
French bond yields climbed further on Tuesday after their biggest daily rise in nearly a month in the previous session, with investors remaining cautious.
The yield on France's 10-year benchmark bond reached 4.96 per cent at one point on Tuesday.
WILL THE UNREST SPREAD TO OTHER COUNTRIES?
If France cannot contain the unrest, there is a risk that it could spill across its borders with deep public anger around Europe over cost-of-living issues.
In neighbouring Italy, clashes erupted between police and protesters on Sunday.
Albania has also seen a series of student demonstrations in recent days over corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, while Spain and Portugal have faced protests over housing.
HOW WILL THE UNREST AFFECT THE 2027 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION?
Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power.
The unrest is likely to boost far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in polls and has long talked tough on law and order.
"Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp, told Reuters.
"It's not just a clear path ahead of her, it's a six-lane highway."
Hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has come under pressure for backing protesters' demands, criticising the government's handling and not clearly condemning the violence.
Meanwhile, Macron, who headed off to the Middle East on Monday, has emerged from the crisis further weakened.
His former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, now a centre-right presidential candidate, said on X he wanted "decisions and initiatives" from the lame-duck leader to "restore order."
ARE PARIS AND OTHER CITIES SAFE TO VISIT?

There have been no reports of any injuries to foreigners caught up in the unrest. However, several European governments advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution.
* The article is from Reuters

d638d300d1e4a46a: Enterprises say nearly a third of their software budgets goes on upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes they wouldn't have chosen, according to research suggesting that keeping vendors happy has become an expensive business.

The study, conducted by Censuswide for software support provider Origina and published with Thinkers50, surveyed 2,018 senior IT decision-makers in the US and UK. Respondents put the average share at 28 percent.

And customers aren't necessarily getting anything better for their money. Some 95 percent of respondents said they had paid for at least one vendor-driven change in the past three years despite expecting worse reliability, performance, or value.
The most recent vendor-driven change cost respondents' organizations an average of $12.87 million.
Origina calls this the "software tax," but unlike most taxes, it comes with the added pleasure of potentially making your IT systems worse.

The costs don't stop at software either. According to the survey, 91 percent of respondents said their organizations had retired working hardware in the past three years to meet software support deadlines, sacrificing an estimated 1.65 years of remaining useful life on average.

Then there's the small matter of finding people to carry out all these supposedly essential changes. Some 84 percent said experienced engineers were regularly diverted from other projects to handle vendor-driven upgrades and migrations.

That leaves less time for the work businesses actually want done, including the AI projects that software vendors themselves have spent the past few years telling everyone they urgently need. Asked about the last time an AI or data project was delayed, paused, or canceled, 90 percent said vendor-driven costs contributed at least moderately.

While customers might be tempted to tell their suppliers where to stick their next upgrade, many apparently don't feel they have much choice. Some 76 percent said they have little negotiating leverage with their major software vendors.
Origina founder and CEO Tomás O'Leary reckons customers have been backed into a corner.

"When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response. That's exactly the problem," he said. "The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded."

The findings also suggest that IT bosses are getting rather fed up with the arrangement. Some 91 percent backed legislation that would give enterprise software customers protections comparable to those enjoyed by long-term residential tenants, while 82 percent supported software maintenance requirements similar to EU hardware repairability rules.
Origina has a commercial interest in the argument: it sells independent support for enterprise software, offering customers an alternative to vendors' own maintenance and upgrade arrangements.
Still, the findings suggest plenty of customers feel they're spending millions following their suppliers' priorities rather than their own. ®
321ede76c371deae: ROM: Tentera Itali merancang menghantar 500 lagi anggota tentera ke Milan, ibu kota kewangan negara itu susulan rusuhan serius, lapor Agensi Berita Jerman (dpa).

475766dcc229314b: MANAMA: French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Gulf, the French presidency said on Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tonnes per month from the Emirates, while an additional 100,000 tonnes monthly will be secured during the stop in Bahrain, the Elysee Palace said.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tonnes per month, representing just over 10 percent of its consumption, the presidency added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France, after a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs.
The French president arrived in Manama on Tuesday and was greeted by crowds of schoolchildren waving Bahraini and French flags.
The trip also included stops in the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar, all of which have been thrown into turmoil by the US-Iran war since February.
Crude oil prices have ballooned during the eight-month conflict, as Iran blockades the Strait of Hormuz – the main exit route for the Gulf's energy exports – with diesel prices among the hardest hit.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to draw up to 100 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves to ease pressure.
Kuwait has also given "very clear commitments" to deliver diesel and kerosene to the French overseas territories of Mayotte and Reunion in the Indian Ocean, the French presidency said.
The shipments will be sent via Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, it added.
Experts have questioned whether the shipments would have an impact on prices, given the risks of renewed fighting in the region.
Talks are underway with countries in the region to bring down maritime insurance prices so that companies can ship greater quantities through the strait at lower cost, the Elysee said.

Presidential advisers expressed satisfaction with the quantity of diesel secured, while Patrick Pouyanne, head of French oil giant TotalEnergies who is on the trip, said the deals would "reassure the French."
"We are not going to run out of diesel in February," he added.
France has also released 10 million barrels of diesel from its reserves, with the aim of cutting prices by 12 to 18 cents, or around five to eight per cent, from next month.

31cd6d1893649711: PETALING JAYA: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has advised Malaysians against using popular navigation app Waze, which was founded in Israel.

Google bought Waze in June 2013 for approximately US$1.15 billion. The app was originally founded in Israel in 2008 by three Israeli entrepreneurs.

2da903bad9cde08b: Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon.

This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover.
Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year.
Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform.

Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole.
What we know about SBC4 so far

The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it.
No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried.

What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat.

Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up.

Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data.
However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running.

Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body.
Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar.

Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission.
Hardening SBC4 for the Moon

The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute.
But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives.
The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1.

“It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.”

However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.”
While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery.

Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself.

“At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained.
At the edge of the edge
FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions.

The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy.

Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images.
For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said.
Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally.

“It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said.

Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call.

"There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space."

Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable.
Despite this, executives and administrators at HPE, Astrolab, Kioxia, and NASA believe that space-based datacenters are still feasible long term.
FLIP
HPE’s Spaceborne Computer 4 will be one of several payloads aboard the FLIP rover.

FLIP will be the largest rover launched by the US since the Apollo program’s manned Moon buggy. And it is by no means small. Designed by Astrolab while measuring roughly 7 feet (2.13 meters) in length and weighing about half a ton, the rover is packed to the gills with cameras, sensors, and even a projector which will eventually be used in place of LCDs on future manned missions to the lunar surface.

For FLIP’s purposes, it’ll mostly be used to project partners' logos onto the Moon’s surface as a sorta advertising gimmick to keep the lights on back at Astrolab’s facilities in Hawthorne while it works on its FLEX rover, which Matthews characterizes as a sort of F150 or Caterpillar tractor for the Moon.

Beyond the scientific equipment, solar panels, and radiators, arguably FLIP’s most striking feature is its disproportionately large wheels. Developed by Venturi Space, along with the rover’s battery pack, these wheels are designed to function much like a pneumatic tire, just without air or rubber. Their size is also intentional. The same wheels found on FLIP are intended for use on NASA’s CLV-1 rover, which is slated to launch in 2028.
Much like FLIP offers HPE as a proving ground to test its lunar compute platform, the rover will do the same for Venturi’s wheels.
Spaceborne Computer 4 and FLIP are slated to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket later this year and will fly to the Moon’s south pole by Astrobotic’s Griffin-1 lander.

Griffin is classified as a medium class lander measuring roughly 15 feet around and 6.5 feet tall (that’s about 4.5 and 2 meters for those of you living in a nation civilized enough to use metric outside the sciences).

The lander is equipped with seven main engines responsible for everything from trans-lunar injection, trajectory correction, lunar orbit insertion, and powered descent to the surface. Four clusters of attitude control thrusters, meanwhile, will (hopefully) keep the thing pointed the right way up.
FLIP is expected to touch down near the Mons Mouton area along the edge of the South Pole before the end of the year. ®
b64bb32658eb7088: BERLIN: US tech giant Amazon on Tuesday announced plans to invest over €16 billion (US$18 billion) in Germany next year, including in data centres and other infrastructure underpinning the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.
The news, unveiled at a business summit hosted by the government in Berlin, is a boost for Europe's struggling top economy as it hunts for new investments, particularly in high-tech fields.

"Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe," said David Zapolsky, Amazon's chief global affairs and legal officer, noting that the firm had already invested over €100 billion in Germany since 2010.
Economy minister Katherina Reiche said Amazon's investments would "strengthen Germany's position in international technology competition and create value and jobs in the process".
Of the €16 billion, nearly five billion will go towards expanding operations of the company's cloud computing division, Amazon Web Services, in the Frankfurt area, as demand grows for AI services.
Some of the investments would go into Amazon Leo, which aims to provide high-speed internet via a network of satellites.
Amazon's warehouses will be upgraded, including through the use of more robotics, and video service Amazon Prime plans to film a slate of new productions in Germany, the firm said.
The investment summit, wrapping up Tuesday, is bringing together more than 200 corporate leaders from Germany and abroad.

The government is seeking to attract more companies to expand their operations and help get the stagnating economy back on its feet, despite frequent complaints about onerous red tape, high energy costs and a lack of skilled labour.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the event his coalition had "embarked on the most ambitious reform and modernisation drive of the past decades. We are committed to seeing these reforms through."
He listed tax relief, cutting bureaucracy and strengthening financial markets as among the key aims.
Earlier, Reiche said in a radio interview that companies had so far pledged investments totalling more than €220 billion at the summit.
Merz opened the event late Monday, holding an on-stage discussion with Jensen Huang, CEO of AI chip giant Nvidia.
At the same time, Berlin announced a partnership with Nvidia aimed at accelerating the use of AI in industrial applications - an area where manufacturing giant Germany hopes that it can excel.

95559f9f2b84b346: PETALING JAYA: Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan) menyeru ahli dan penyokong parti-parti yang sehaluan dengan Perikatan Nasional (PN) supaya bertenang, susulan keputusan Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM) membatalkan pendaftaran PN.
Presiden Hamzah Zainudin berkata Wawasan menolak keputusan JPPM sepenuhnya, dan bersama 'parti-parti politik sahabat PN' akan mempertahankan hak melalui saluran undang-undang.
Awal hari ini, JPPM mengumumkan pembatalan pendaftaran PN selepas mendapati penjelasan dikemukakan gabungan itu gagal menyangkal asas pembatalan dalam notis terdahulu.

Pembatalan ini menyusuli penggantungan semua kegiatan PN pada 23 Sept. Pada 13 Okt, Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur membenarkan PN mendapatkan kebenaran memulakan prosiding semakan kehakiman bagi mencabar dua notis dikeluarkan JPPM, namun tidak membenarkan penangguhan sementara terhadap penggantungan aktiviti PN. "Segala tindakan undang-undang seperti yang dijelaskan oleh Setiausaha Agung PN, Takiyuddin Hassan, akan diteruskan," kata Hamzah dalam kenyataan.

Siasatan JPPM terhadap PN dibuat susulan aduan dilaporkan Bersatu yang mendakwa mereka dinafikan hak untuk menghadiri, memberi pendapat dan mengundi di dalam mesyuarat majlis tertinggi PN pada 16 Jul.
Awal hari ini, Takiyuddin mengumumkan PN mempertimbangkan untuk merayu kepada menteri dalam negeri bagi mencabar tindakan JPPM, selain daripada proses perundangan.
Takiyuddin juga mengumumkan parti-parti komponen PN masih boleh bertanding pada PRN Melaka, 14 Nov ini, menggunakan lambang parti anggota.
Berkaitan PRN Melaka, Hamzah berkata parti-parti yang sehaluan dengan PN akan memasuki pilihan raya dengan strategi yang tepat.
"Sehubungan itu, seluruh ahli dan penyokong diseru supaya kekal tenang dan mematuhi lunas perundangan dalam negara," katanya.
Dalam pada itu, Hamzah mendakwa pembatalan pendaftaran PN dibuat berdasarkan dua tafsiran berbeza oleh JPPM dalam pemakaian Seksyen 18C Akta Pertubuhan.
Menurut Hamzah, pada 13 Julai, empat Ahli Parlimen Bersatu membuat aduan kepada JPPM yang mempersoalkan kuorum mesyuarat majlis pimpinan tertinggi Bersatu.
Katanya, dalam jawapan pada 16 Julai, JPPM merujuk Seksyen 18C Akta Pertubuhan dan menetapkan bahawa keputusan parti politik berhubung urusan dalaman adalah muktamad.
Katanya lagi, JPPM turut menyerahkan perkara tersebut untuk diputuskan secara dalaman mengikut perlembagaan parti, dan menegaskan bahawa JPPM tidak mempunyai kuasa untuk campur tangan.
Sebaliknya, JPPM mentafsir sendiri Fasal 7.1 Perlembagaan PN dan menolak tafsiran PN, berhubung aduan Bersatu, katanya.
"Undang-undang yang sama, jabatan yang sama, tetapi tafsiran yang berbeza mengikut pihak yang terlibat," katanya.

Hamzah juga mendakwa keputusan pembatalan hari ini bertentangan dengan pendirian JPPM yang terkandung dalam surat bertarikh 6 Okt, yang menyatakan bahawa isu-isu yang dibangkitkan oleh PN akan dijawab di mahkamah.

c2fadc428199286f: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru.
According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data.

On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server.
"Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF].
ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru.

"ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'."
The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second.

"The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added.

"ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years."

The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory.
The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements.

"Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands.

"The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ®

c7a7043d35fec3f5: WANGARATTA (Australia), Oct 20 — A rural Australian town felt a mix of horror and disbelief today after a highly respected lawmaker was gravely injured in what looked to be a targeted attack.
Former nurse and midwife Helen Haines entered parliament in 2019, earning respect across the political divide for her efforts to stamp out corruption and bolster transparency.
The 65-year-old was struck by a two-tonne SUV in Wangaratta yesterday afternoon, suffering critical injuries in what authorities described as a “deliberate” act of violence.
Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant said a sombre mood had settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250 kilometres northeast of state capital Melbourne.
“Helen was well respected. She was diligent and hard working,” Grant told AFP.
“What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can’t believe it, people are horrified by what has happened.”
Haines — who lives on a small cattle property outside Wangaratta — was getting something from the trunk of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser.
Authorities said the 43-year-old man turned the car around before veering at Haines and pinning her against her own vehicle.
The driver then allegedly reversed before ramming her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
‘Devastated’
Police have said little about the alleged attacker’s motive.
Locals, meanwhile, are struggling to comprehend why anyone would wish harm on the well-liked Haines.
Florist Jess Woodrow said Haines was a friendly face who would pop into the store when she was not tied up in the capital Canberra.
“We are absolutely devastated to hear what has happened. Helen was a beautiful person. She didn’t have a bad bone in her body,” Woodrow told AFP.
“It’s the last thing you would think would happen here.”
Haines entered parliament as an independent lawmaker in 2019, representing the sprawling seat of Indi.
She was a popular representative, holding the seat at the 2025 election with a hefty margin of more than 18,000 votes.
Haines was a vocal champion for greater climate action, better rural healthcare, and help for struggling small businesses.
The First Peoples’ Assembly of Victoria said Haines was a “staunch supporter” of Indigenous rights as well.
But it was her work to hold politicians to account that perhaps earned Haines the most respect both inside and outside parliament.
“Helen Haines is characterised by her kindness, her compassion, her diligence, her intelligence,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.
“She’s someone who is such a strong advocate and is widely respected right across the political spectrum because the way that she advocates is very respectful.” — AFP
f382bc1ee56d8f38: BOGOTÁ, Oct 20 — Ahead of an election that could return the right to power in Brazil, polls show support slipping for recently elected conservative leaders across Latin America.

New surveys in Peru, Colombia, Chile and Argentina suggest voters are losing patience with governments elected on promises to curb crime, revive weak economies and forge closer ties with US President Donald Trump.
Peru’s conservative President Keiko Fujimori and her hardline, gun-toting Colombian counterpart, Abelardo de la Espriella, are the latest newcomers to see their ratings fall.

An Ipsos poll last week showed approval of Fujimori dropping to 40 percent from 57 percent when she took office in August, while De la Espriella’s fell more than three points in his first month in office.

In Chile, where voters elected their most conservative president in three decades last year amid concerns over organized crime, one-quarter of President Jose Antonio Kast’s supporters say they regret backing him, according to the left-wing Fundacion Nodo XXI.
Argentine President Javier Milei, a hero to free-market conservatives across the region, has also seen his ratings hit record lows a year before seeking re-election.

“I think a lot of these governments raised expectations probably unrealistically. People want quick results, which are impossible to produce,” Michael Shifter, senior fellow at The Inter-American Dialogue think tank in Washington, told AFP.
But the backlash has little to do with ideology, he cautioned.
“I’m not sure that if these were governments of the left that it would be any different,” he said.

An AmericasBarometer survey of more than 25,000 people in 21 countries found weak support for the leaders of eight US allies that belong to Trump’s “Shield of the Americas” alliance: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Panama and Paraguay.
‘Concrete action’
Nowhere is impatience for better governance more visible than in Bolivia, where voters dumped the long-ruling socialists in the midst of the country’s worst economic crisis in 40 years.
President Rodrigo Paz was elected as a moderate, pro-business alternative, but was only six months into his mandate when demonstrators demanding his resignation blockaded major cities.
Many blame the 59-year-old for failing to end crippling fuel shortages.
“I thought it would be different, that things were going to change,” Jamil Alanoca, a 19-year-old business student, told AFP.
Across the border in Peru, voters went to the polls in April and June seeking relief from an extortion epidemic and are already showing frustration at the lack of results.
“A problem that has persisted for so many years (insecurity) isn’t going to be solved overnight,” Guillermo Loli, director of opinion polls at Ipsos Peru, told AFP.
But “at least concrete actions should be seen,” he said.
The Bukele exception
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s iron-fisted approach to his country’s gangs has earned him a cult-like following.

The self-described “world’s coolest dictator” enjoys approval of 83 percent, according to the AmericasBarometer survey, after driving crime rates to historic lows through a sweeping anti-gang crackdown.
The gains were achieved by jailing more than 90,000 suspects under a four-year-old state of emergency that rights groups say has been marked by serious abuses.

“Bukele’s El Salvador remains a defining experiment — a state that traded liberties for safety and, by these measures, delivered greater safety,” the 2026 Pulse of Democracy report produced by Vanderbilt University using AmericasBarometer polling said.
Shifter expressed doubt that Bukele’s success against domestic gangs could be replicated against the transnational crime networks operating elsewhere in the region.
“Bukele, I think, is really sui generis, he’s the exception,” he said.
Chilean pensioner Leoncio Silva said he believed that, given more time, Kast would vanquish the foreign gangs blamed for a surge in violence in his country.
“Let’s wait a year and see,” he urged. — AFP
0cc474777a4f8856: BARRANQUILLA (Colombia), Oct 20 — Colombia’s new right-wing leader has built himself a costly new presidential palace — a white-columned mansion far from Bogota that doubles as a political manifesto.

Tucked inside a Caribbean military base, President Abelardo de la Espriella’s new headquarters is meant to embody two of his signature promises: a focus on Colombia’s security forces and shifting power away from a capital accused of neglecting the country’s regions.
The austere neoclassical building, set amid tropical gardens and palm trees in Barranquilla, has quickly become one of the most visible symbols of his presidency.
Admirers see a bold statement of decentralisation from a leader determined to govern from beyond Bogota.
“For a very long time, the coast and the regions outside Bogota have been forgotten,” said Libardo Charris, a 54-year-old furniture merchant in Barranquilla.
The debate has even prompted questions about whether a city of about 1.3 million people is the new seat of power.
De la Espriella has frequently refers to Barranquilla as the “alternative capital.”
Critics dismiss it as an expensive political stage set that has earned the mocking nickname “the Temu White House.”

Constitutional experts say transforming Barranquilla into an official alternative seat of government would be difficult, although some Colombian presidents have occasionally governed from cities outside the capital.
“It is not an alternative capital. It is a place where the president stays for a few days and carries out his functions,” constitutional lawyer Juan Manuel Charry told AFP.
Creating a second capital would require constitutional reform and approval by Congress.
Political price tag
From the streets around the sprawling military compound, little of the mansion can be seen.
The property sits inside a restricted area of more than 50,000 square metres, roughly the size of several soccer fields.
A modest sign outside reads: “Presidency of the Republic. Freedom and Order.”
The mansion has already hosted high-profile visitors, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez.
Military personnel continue their daily routines around the complex, while official vehicles, aides and security details come and go.
The facilities include an underground bunker designed to shelter the president and senior civilian and military officials in a crisis.
An admirer of US President Donald Trump, De la Espriella has bristled at comparisons between his new base and the White House.
Yet social media has filled with memes highlighting the resemblance, while critics accuse him of embracing symbolism over substance.
De la Espriella often works from the compound dressed in tactical clothing, dark glasses and a baseball cap, blending into the military surroundings.
He arrives by helicopter or in convoys of armored vehicles, images regularly showcased on his social media accounts.
Recently he led a security operation in a nearby city carrying a pistol on his belt.
Better known as the hometown of pop star Shakira and for its carnival celebrations than as a center of political power, Barranquilla has found itself unexpectedly at the heart of national politics.
Gabriel Sanchez, a 47-year-old shopkeeper, said he welcomed the fact that Colombia’s Caribbean region was now receiving greater attention. Under De la Espriella, he said, the coast is “more visible.”
Street vendor Darlys Patricia Guerrero, 40, said it was “great” to have a presidential headquarters in the sweltering coastal city rather than the high-altitude capital.
“I’ve never seen the president around here,” she told AFP outside the Paradise Battalion base.

At a time of fiscal strain, opponents question the roughly US$650,000 (RM2.7 million) spent renovating the 1938 mansion, according to the Atlantico province’s governor, as well as the cost of moving presidential operations to Colombia’s Caribbean coast.
The criticism is pointed because De la Espriella, a wealthy former lawyer, won office promising a hard line against crime, a defense of traditional values and a leaner state.
Opponents argue that true decentralization requires transferring resources and decision-making powers to the regions rather than relocating the president’s desk.

“There are two governments: the one shown to the cameras and another behind it that we see in the territories,” said Edwin Capaz Lectamo, an Indigenous leader from the southwestern department of Cauca.
Yet beyond the legal questions, political arguments and online jokes, the Barranquilla headquarters has revived a long-running rivalry between Colombia’s Caribbean coast and the Andean capital.
“There’s more joy, more spontaneity here,” said homemaker Alejandra Diaz, 38, comparing her city with Bogota.

Whether it proves a lasting shift in how Colombia is governed or simply a costly symbol, the white-columned mansion has already achieved one thing: turning a building into a national debate about where power belongs. — AFP

ae74a8939d7a36bf: UPDATED Google Cloud has blamed a “power event” for taking down multiple online products for customers in Western Europe, and is pledging to restore normal service within the hour.
The unplanned downtime for customers began at 0608 UTC when europe-west-2-b, one of three local availability zones in the London region, started playing up.

According to an update on its status page, Google Cloud said at 1158 UTC that full recovery workloads should be “completed, tentatively” by 1300 UTC. Customers can expect another update at that point, with Google either giving the thumbs up, thumbs sideways or having to admit engineers are still working on a fix.

Services that went AWOL included BigQuery Data TransferService, Cloud Filestore, Cloud Run, Google App Engine, Google Cloud NetApp Volumes, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Managed Service for Apache Kafka.
So what caused online services to melt at customers including Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Royal Mail, Rightmove, DPD, BT, Screwfix and Revolut? Power.

"A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritizing the recovery of existing workloads.Customers may not be able to yet create new workloads."
The Register has asked Google for further elucidation but it said the only information is available on the status page.

The "fragility" of the cloud model is again on display, Dr Amro Al-Said Ahmad, a lecturer in computer science at Keele University told The Register. He estimates that a total of 38 services were down and out for the count.

"The incident highlights the dependency effect of modern cloud ecosystems. When a core cloud region experiences failures, the impact extends far beyond the directly affected services. Applications, APIs, databases, authentication systems, payment platforms, analytics pipelines, and third-party SaaS products that depend on those services can all experience cascading failures."

"A problem in a single cloud region can therefore propagate through an entire digital supply chain, affecting organisations that are several layers removed from the original outage. While this is a regional outage centered on europe-west2, the breadth of affected services highlights a key cloud engineering lesson: resilience is not achieved by simply moving to the cloud. True resilience requires designing for regional failures through multi-region deployments, workload portability, and tested disaster recovery procedures."
Updated at 17.37 UTC on October 20, 2026, to add:
Google's status page says it mostly ironed out the wrinkles at 14.03 UTC and normal service resumed for the majority of customers.

"The issue with impacted GCP products has been mitigated for most of the customers and it is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our Engineering Team is working on it."

"No further updates will be provided here. We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we're working on resolving the issue." ®

678424bafb0509cf: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.

As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.
The AI adoption spectrum by industry
Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).
Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing.

While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge.

By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers.
The AI skills workers are being asked to learn

Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn’t previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2).
Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills.

Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting.

One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like.
How early AI adoption helps your career

Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice.

In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth.

Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn’t matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren’t boxed in by them anymore.”
The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn

If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry:
Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0)
Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0)
Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0)
Education: $883 average (42% spent $0)

Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3).
Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve.

Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills.

However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%).
Conclusion

The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations.
This content was produced by TripleTen. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

4775b1c0b0133fdf: Microsoft has been forced to admit that the Always On VPN glitch – which it said it had fixed in an update on October 13 – was not actually fixed after all.

We've all been there. You fix that bug, or tweak the configuration setting, and you're pleased with yourself, but it turns out it didn't take, and you have to send the "er, about that fix" follow-up email of shame.

The same has happened to Microsoft. After proudly declaring the problem resolved as part of its last security update, the company had to roll back its triumphant trumpeting to a sad little parp from a clown's horn in the message WI1482218:
"This disclosure was mistakenly updated to Resolved status on October 13, 2026. We have returned its status to Mitigated.
"We apologize for any inconvenience or confusion."

The bug in question concerns the operating system's Always On VPN functionality, a useful bit of code that quietly opens a VPN connection in the background without tiresome prompts for authentication. It dates back to Windows 10, and Microsoft alerted administrators to problems after the September 2026 Windows security update inadvertently broke it.
The issue affects Windows 11 versions from 24H2 through 26H2.

The problem could occur when the VPN was set to try a different connection method if the initial connection failed (Microsoft gave the example of using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP).

According to Microsoft: "Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use'."

This is not ideal for administrators. The workaround Microsoft highlighted back on October 13 was to change from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, which would at least get affected users up and running.
The workaround remains the same. The bad news is that, because last week's fix did not work, affected administrators will need to apply the workaround for a bit longer.
Microsoft claimed, "A resolution for this issue is planned to be included in an update to be released in the coming weeks." ®

29c1a61ab8cec165: Britain's national digital ID scheme may be dead, but Whitehall appears to have forgotten to tell the infrastructure.

Despite the government scrapping its controversial plans, officials told MPs on Monday that work continues on GOV.UK One Login, digital wallets, and a growing collection of digital credentials designed to help people prove who they are.

The abandoned scheme was one of Keir Starmer's flagship policies, originally pitched as a compulsory digital ID card to crack down on illegal working. Privacy campaigners weren't impressed, warning of surveillance and government overreach, and ministers eventually made it voluntary before Andy Burnham, decided to bin the whole thing.

But scrapping the scheme hasn't dented Whitehall's digital identity ambitions. Officials told MPs this week that more than 80 types of documents are earmarked for the government's digital wallet, including proof of benefits, driving test certificates, and Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) certificates. That's quite a lot of paperwork for something that's supposedly dead.
The revelations came during a Public Accounts Committee hearing on Monday, where MPs wanted to know what exactly had been scrapped.

"But is it not the case, based on the answers you've given us this afternoon, that the infrastructure of digital ID in the public sector is still being pursued?" asked Sarah Green, Liberal Democrat MP for Chesham and Amersham.

Susannah Storey, DCMS permanent secretary, was keen to draw a line between the national scheme ministers had scrapped and the digital identity projects Whitehall had no intention of abandoning. One Login already allows people to prove who they are online, she said, but "that is not the same as a national digital identity strategy."

Rod Latham, DCMS director for cybersecurity and digital identity, had a convenient explanation for why so much of digital ID was still standing: the government had only scrapped plans for a new identity product.
"We already had One Login and the Gov Wallet," he told MPs, adding that work on the digital identity trust framework was also underway before the national scheme was announced.
Whitehall isn't wasting time putting that technology to use, with officials confirming that testing is already underway to enable digital credentials to work with private businesses.

Natalie Jones, the senior responsible owner for GOV.UK One Login, revealed that the government had opened a testing environment for private sector providers to integrate with its digital wallet technology. This would let people use digital driving licenses to prove their age in pubs, collect parcels, or verify their identity online.

"We've got a bit of a chicken and egg situation. A digital driving license is only useful if there are people ready and shops and businesses ready to receive it,” Jones said, noting that further testing is planned for December, with a national rollout of digital driving licenses targeted for 2027.
MPs also pressed officials on privacy, particularly whether citizens would have to consent before their information was shared between government departments.
"In the confines of digital ID used in digital services, then consent is the model," said Christine Bellamy, interim director general for digital products at the Government Digital Service.
There's a catch, of course. Government departments can already share data without asking permission, and officials couldn't quite explain how that squares with their promises about consent.
"The strategy needs to be fully finished," Bellamy admitted, which might not be the reassurance MPs were hoping for.

Jones insisted that One Login was "not a big data lake," saying it stores identity information separately and cannot see what users do inside government services. "One Login does not issue a single identifier to people," she added.
Rupert Lowe MP remained unconvinced, warning that Britain could end up getting digital ID "by the back door rather than the front door."
Officials maintained that the canceled national scheme was fundamentally different from the services still being developed, and that people would retain alternatives to digital identification.
National digital ID may be officially dead, but between One Login, digital wallets, and dozens of planned credentials, Whitehall still has plenty of identity-related work to keep it busy. ®

4b11a3faaa1b7c93: Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.

He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.

On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.

In late June of 2013, a lightning strike sparked a fire in this stretch of mostly treeless tundra, in the northern backcountry of the park. Whipped by the Chinooks, intense downslope winds created as moist ocean air surmounts and then descends the Alaska Range, the fire ripped across nearly 35,000 acres. It burned through much of the vegetation and deep into the topsoil, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves the frozen permafrost, a massive storehouse of carbon that underlies 85% of Alaska.

During their first survey, in 2016, the researchers found that in places where the fire burned hottest and deepest, the thawed soil above the permafrost (known as the active layer) extended between a foot and nearly two feet deeper than in plots outside the burn scar—an indication of deep thawing.
JAMES TEMPLE

Crucially, the fire also crossed two sets of survey grids that the National Park Service established in 2001, including the one where the researchers stood that morning. That pre-fire snapshot offered the Northern Arizona group a rare opportunity to study how the blaze has altered the vegetation, carbon, and permafrost across time, says Xanthe Walker, one of the principal investigators on the project, who was watching over Haverdink’s work that morning.
These direct observations from high-latitude fires are helping scientists to better understand the impacts of wildfire and permafrost loss on climate change, she says.
“There’s a lot of uncertainty,” Walker says. “These are huge biomes with massive fires that no one’s ever been to or ever looked at.”

They’re among a growing group of researchers striving to untangle what happens in the aftermath of fires in the Arctic-boreal region as they occur more often, burn hotter than before, and expose the landscape and frozen permafrost to a warming climate.

The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects: As warming temperatures fuel more frequent and severe fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires, and permafrost loss.

Understanding just how powerful these effects are, how they compound, and to what degree other transformations of the landscape may mitigate them is essential to gain a clearer picture of our climate future.

Notably, past modeling suggested that the carbon dioxide uptake from expanding trees and plants may largely offset the release of carbon from warming soils and melting permafrost, at least over long periods and under moderate levels of warming. But the improving observations and analyses have revealed worrisome signs about the impacts of rising Arctic-boreal emissions in the immediate decades ahead, as the world struggles to keep global warming within relatively safe boundaries.
The permafrost problem

Permafrost makes up 15% of the land surface of the Northern Hemisphere and holds about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. Most of it formed during the last ice age, but it’s been thawing at an accelerating rate during the last half-century, amid rising temperatures and worsening fires. As it melts, microbes begin to break down that organic matter, releasing it into the air in the form of carbon dioxide and methane. Both are powerful greenhouse gases that fuel climate change.

The impacts of permafrost loss, however, aren’t as straightforward as they may initially seem. Notably, there has been a long-running scientific debate over what would have the strongest effect on the exchange of greenhouse gases over the next few centuries: the loss of carbon in soil and permafrost or the carbon uptake from so-called “Arctic greening,” which describes the spread of carbon-absorbing plants across the landscape as temperatures rise.

Thawing permafrost itself can contribute to the latter phenomenon as the unfrozen soil layer deepens and makes more nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients accessible to plants. Carbon-sucking trees and shrubs with deeper root systems can take hold and thrive in places where they wouldn’t have been able to in the past.
MIKHAIL KANEVSKIY; UNIVERSITY OF ALASKA FAIRBANKS

But as more Arctic-boreal fires ignite and more permafrost melts, researchers have been able to closely study what exactly happens in the aftermath, using on-site surveys like those conducted by the Northern Arizona University team, satellite observations, lidar flights, a widening network of greenhouse-gas-measuring towers, and other tools.
The findings have alarmed many researchers.

In particular, permafrost seems particularly prone to abrupt thawing rather than the gradual version that major climate models have simulated. A 2020 paper found that this could release far more carbon than previously understood, doubling the emissions from thawing permafrost and offsetting the carbon uptake from future plant growth.
In addition, even if carbon levels eventually net out through Arctic greening, the emissions from high-latitude fires and permafrost loss appear to be accelerating warming right now.

Susan Natali, an Arctic climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, and her colleagues have published several papers in recent years concluding that the combined emissions from these feedback effects will push the planet past 2 °C faster than currently predicted. She and other researchers also found that about 40% of the Arctic-boreal zone has already flipped from a carbon sink into a carbon source, when the emissions from permafrost melting, fires and other forces are taken into account.

“The more we learn about processes like abrupt thaw, deeper-burning fires, and cold-season emissions, and the more we see disturbances increasing, the more likely it is that the sink will weaken and source areas will expand,” Natali said in an email.
But there’s still considerable uncertainty about the differences between the ways fires and thawing permafrost might alter landscapes, under different circumstances in different biomes.
“This is just a challenge of the science, because it’s really hard to measure such a huge area, which is not one system,” she says. “It’s many, many, many, many different types of ecosystems.”
Results may vary

The Northern Arizona University researchers have been at the forefront of efforts to study the aftermath of intensifying fires across different parts of Alaska. Over the last two decades, Michelle Mack, a professor of ecosystem ecology who was previously Walker’s postdoctoral advisor, has overseen repeat survey work on fire sites across forests and tundras, from the relatively warm southern interior to the frigid North Slope.
MATT ‘MARTIAN’ WILLIAMS

Her husband and frequent collaborator, Ted Schuur, is also a professor at the university and oversees several permafrost monitoring and experimental research sites at the Eight Mile Lake study area, just north of Denali National Park.

If there’s a single takeaway from the body of science that the Northern Arizona scientists have produced, it’s this: It’s complicated. The local climate and ecosystem, the severity of the fires that have occurred, the type of permafrost, and numerous other factors can substantially shift the uptake or loss of carbon, the amount of permafrost that’s thawed, the extent to which it may recover, and the future flammability of the landscape.

In one early study, the researchers and their collaborators surveyed dozens of stands dominated by black spruce trees in the aftermath of a series of large boreal fires in 2004, between the Brooks Range and the Alaska Range. One of the notable findings: Severe burns that left little behind of the decaying organic matter in the topsoil induced a shift toward faster-growing and less flammable deciduous trees. The sites where deciduous trees dominated stored about five times as much soil carbon as stands that returned to black spruce, Mack, Walker, and their coauthors noted in a 2021 Science paper.
That means the subsequent uptake of carbon on those stands “more than compensated” for the amount released in the initial fire, Walker says.
GETTY IMAGES

But the 2007 Anaktuvuk River tundra fire, which remains the largest fire on record in Alaska’s North Slope, offers a starkly different case study. In the initial analysis there, Mack, Schuur, and their coauthors found that the fire released more than 2 million tons of carbon to the atmosphere, basically negating the amount that tundra ecosystems around the world removed from the air that year.

Subsequent studies found that more than a third of the scorched landscape sank, slid, and crumpled as the ice wedges below collapsed, the telltale signs of abrupt permafrost melting. Nearly two decades later, much of that thawed, decaying organic matter continues to release carbon dioxide and methane in the most severely burned patches of the fire scar, says Adrian Rocha, an associate professor at the University of Notre Dame.

It will take decades to centuries to recover all the carbon lost there, if ever happens at all, according to Rocha, who continues to monitor the site using Eddy covariance flux towers, which measure the exchange of greenhouse gases between Earth and atmosphere.

Mack says these on-the-ground measurements are critical to understanding what sorts of ecosystems recover, which shift into new states, whether they release a lot of carbon or a little, and when and where plant growth can offset that.
That said, the stakes of thawing permafrost are clear.

“If we step back as ecosystem ecologists, we know that there’s a lot more carbon stored below ground in permafrost than there is above ground in vegetation,” she says. “If permafrost carbon is released, it could swamp all of these other interesting details.”
In the lab

The Northern Arizona University research team shipped a pallet of soil samples back from Denali. The material included plugs of moss and decaying plant matter known as “brownies,” as well as permafrost cores and samples of the unfrozen soil layer. In the months since, they’ve cut, dried, weighed, combusted and analyzed various samples and inputted their field and lab findings into databases.
JAMES TEMPLE

Walker says they’re exploring a variety of research questions, including how much that top organic layer has recovered since the initial post-fire survey and how much carbon has been lost and recovered since the fire.
The analysis is still underway, but in the most severely burned sites, it appears that the thawed layer of soil above the permafrost remain deeper some 13 years.
“Thaw still reaches further into the soil each summer than it probably did before the fire, which exposes more soil to decomposition,” Walker explained in an email.
They’re now hoping to use lab analyses to determine how much of that carbon is being lost.
Stepping into the climate future
On my last afternoon in Healy, Alaska, I followed Schuur along a narrow walkway of wooden boards suspended above a tundra field just north of Denali, hoping to get a glimpse into our climate future.

In 2008, he and his research team devised a way to subject permafrost to the temperature levels expected two or three decades from now by setting up snow fences around dozens of designated research plots. That allowed extra snow to build up—which, counterintuitively, acts like a blanket, adding thermal insulation during the winter that kept the test plots warmer than the controls.

Over the course of the 13-year experiment, the soil carbon levels in those 10-by-10-meter plots declined by 23%, Schuur and his coauthors found. The land collapsed in many of the sites, forming craters several feet deep.

As I stepped heel-to-toe along the planks into the middle of one plot, I descended about four feet, experiencing subsidence in three dimensions. Looking up at the edge from the walkway, I felt as if I were diaphragm deep in an empty pool.
JAMES TEMPLE

Schuur, though, had another thing to show me. As we crested a ridge between plots, he pointed down to a shallower—though no less obvious—pool on the other side. It was a control site that had melted and collapsed on its own, without any assistance from simulated warming or fires.
“Every plot is just going off in its own trajectory,” he said. “This stuff is happening because the whole place is warming … and all these changes just go faster if you first burn the surface.”
Schuur expects that the permafrost underlying the whole field will thaw deeply by the end of 2040.
“There won’t be any surface permafrost based on our current warming,” he says.

Unless the world radically cuts emissions and gets fires under control, this same phenomenon will creep up the state, decade by decade, until even the permafrost under Alaska’s North Slope sinks to similar depths and gives up the carbon it has held for millennia.

"The way this works in aviation is that you not only want to learn about the serious crashes where someone has in fact died; you want to learn about the near-misses, because you can learn from those and help avoid them in the future," he said.

However, the government has yet to commit to adding AI-specific measures to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. Alexandra Jones, Director General for Growth, Science and International at the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, told MPs last week that amendments remain under consideration.

In January, the House of Commons Treasury Committee called on financial regulators to conduct stress tests to ensure businesses are ready for AI-driven market shocks. The committee said there should be clear lines of accountability when AI systems produce harmful or unfair outcomes. ®
